svg.text: WHO My Five Moments for Hand Hygiene
1 BEFORE touching a patient
Protects the PATIENT from germs on your hands
2 BEFORE a clean or aseptic procedure
Protects the PATIENT from their own germs entering
3 AFTER body fluid exposure risk
Protects YOU — and do it even after removing gloves
4 AFTER touching a patient
Protects you and the environment
5 AFTER touching patient surroundings
Moment 5 is the one everybody fails
You adjusted the drip stand.
You did not touch the patient.
You still clean your hands.
The bed rail, the notes, the pump and the
locker are all inside the patient zone,
and they all carry the patient's organisms.
Moments 1 and 2 protect the patient.
Moments 3, 4 and 5 protect you and
everybody else on the ward.
Rub or wash? The rule that decides
ALCOHOL HAND RUB — the default
Faster, kinder to skin, more effective on most
organisms. 20 to 30 seconds. Use when hands
are visibly clean.
SOAP AND WATER — required when:
hands are visibly soiled or contaminated
after using the toilet
after caring for a patient with DIARRHOEA
Alcohol does NOT kill Clostridioides difficile
spores or norovirus. Only the friction and
running water physically remove them.
Technique and the things that defeat it
Wet, soap, six steps, rinse, dry — 40 to 60 seconds.
Palms · backs · between fingers · backs of fingers
· thumbs · fingertips into the palm
The missed areas, every time:
FINGERTIPS and THUMBS
— and they are what touch the patient most.
What must come off before you start
Rings with stones, wrist watch, bracelets,
long or artificial nails, chipped varnish.
Sleeves bare below the elbow. Cover any cut
with a waterproof dressing before the shift.
